source_refs.note: Exercise 14.3, Question 12: (u + v) x (u - v) = -2(u x v) (book p.283). Proof, no key answer.

blocks.prompt: 12. Use the definition of cross product, prove that for any vectors \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\): \((\underline{u} + \underline{v}) \times (\underline{u} - \underline{v}) = -2(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\)
blocks.explanation:
A proof using the properties that follow from the definition.
We must expand the product of two brackets.
Plan: distributive law (Question 7 (iv)), \(\underline{x} \times \underline{x} = \underline{0}\) and \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u} = -\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\) (Question 7 (ii)).
steps:
Given: any vectors \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}\).
To prove: \((\underline{u} + \underline{v}) \times (\underline{u} - \underline{v}) = -2(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\).
Method: Expand like a product of brackets in algebra, but keep the order of every cross product; then use the properties proved from the definition in Question 7.

Expand the brackets
\[(\underline{u} + \underline{v}) \times (\underline{u} - \underline{v})\]
\[= \underline{u} \times \underline{u} - \underline{u} \times \underline{v}\]
\[+\ \underline{v} \times \underline{u} - \underline{v} \times \underline{v}\]
Why: Distributive law on both sides (and \((-1)\) comes out of a cross product, Question 7 (iii)).

Simplify
\[= \underline{0} - \underline{u} \times \underline{v} - \underline{u} \times \underline{v} - \underline{0}\]
\[= -2(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\]
Why: \(\underline{u} \times \underline{u} = \underline{v} \times \underline{v} = \underline{0}\) because the angle is 0 and \(\sin 0 = 0\); \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u} = -\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\).

Check with an example
\[\underline{u} = \underline{i},\ \underline{v} = \underline{j}\]
\[(\underline{i} + \underline{j}) \times (\underline{i} - \underline{j}) = -\underline{k} - \underline{k} = -2\underline{k}\]
\[-2(\underline{i} \times \underline{j}) = -2\underline{k}\]
Why: \(\underline{i} \times \underline{j} = \underline{k}\), \(\underline{j} \times \underline{i} = -\underline{k}\), \(\underline{i} \times \underline{i} = \underline{j} \times \underline{j} = \underline{0}\); both sides are \(-2\underline{k}\).
